source.title: Parts-of-Speech as Emergent Categories in SAE Latent Space
source.authors: Alessandro Bondielli; Lucia C. Passaro; Serena Auriemma; Alessandro Lenci

page_placements.theme: Concepts carried by groups of SAE latents, with single latents serving several related categories (not neurons)

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes POS information in SAE latents, not whether individual neuron poles have a human-nameable main job or whether neuron explanations predict held-out activations. Its results concern a related but different construct, so it neither tests nor directly challenges the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports distributed POS-category patterns in SAE latents, but POS categories are not tests of neuron-pole job explanations. These results are recorded under versions ["none"]. Per-tag figures without stated numeric values are not assigned invented values. The paper's random-label control and dense-activation baselines concern POS probing, not the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study examines SAE latents (EleutherAI sae-llama-3-8b-32x on LLaMA-3-8B), not the model's own neurons or neuron poles. It probes how part-of-speech information is organized. It reports no share of neurons with one, two or unknown jobs, no scaling or architecture comparison, no InceptionV1 analysis, no neuron attribution graphs, and no simulation scoring of neuron explanations. It neither tests nor uses the claim. It does not cite the essay or the OpenAI neuron-explanation paper. It touches on monosemanticity only in general terms.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find POS distinctions recoverable from SAE activations and carried by compact but distributed, category-dependent latent groups. These groups are stable on held-out data but overlap across categories and partly track lexical and positional cues. The authors note the evidence is predictive, not causal. They add that latent-level interpretability claims should be checked against grounded category inventories, not top-activating examples alone.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses POS probing, coefficient-based latent salience, coverage, and held-out validation on SAE representations, rather than explaining neuron poles with natural-language descriptions and testing those explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer affects reported results: mean distinctiveness is 0.15±0.03 at layer 2, 0.32±0.09 at layer 15, and 0.27±0.07 at layer 30. The paper also reports slight layer variation and depth-wise redistribution of which latents are selected.

fits_no_version.finding: POS categories in LLaMA-3-8B SAE space are carried by compact groups of latents rather than single latents. The union of these groups is 498 latents, 12% of them shared across 2+ POS tags.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LLaMA-3-8B SAE representations, POS information is localized in category-dependent groups of latents that overlap across categories, not a one-latent-per-category mapping.

fits_no_version.finding: The selected groups fire on held-out target tokens (recall mostly ≥0.95) but are only partly distinctive: mean D 0.27 against a 0.06 chance level.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: POS-related SAE latent groups generalize to held-out tokens but also co-activate on other POS categories.

fits_no_version.finding: On controlled sentences the groups show high recall (0.937) and low precision (0.192), varying by template, with a first-token latent confound.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: POS latent groups are active but not selective on controlled examples.

fits_no_version.finding: Distinctiveness and compact-classifier scores change modestly across layers 2, 15 and 30, while L* size stays about 500.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: POS organization in this SAE is broadly layer-stable, with depth-wise redistribution of latents.

fits_no_version.finding: Several top-coefficient latents recur across closed-class categories (e.g., 72975 in AUX/CCONJ/PART); the authors call them possibly polyfunctional (App. B.1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some highly POS-salient SAE latents serve several grammatical categories.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The study analyzes one base language model and one SAE, on English POS categories. Its localization uses linear-probe coefficients, which the authors say are predictive rather than causal evidence. The controlled dataset is small and limited mainly to nouns and verbs. Some cited performance plots do not provide exact per-category values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No per-POS figure-only values were extracted because the text does not state their numeric values. Results of the random-label control and raw-activation probing baselines were omitted because they address POS probing confounds and comparisons, not any claim version.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron audit and no shares of poles with one, two or unknown jobs.
One model and one SAE only. No neuron-level shares across models or scale.
No InceptionV1 or classic polysemantic neuron reanalysis.
No comparison of architectures, regularization or tools against interpretable-neuron share.
No natural-language neuron explanations tested on where neurons fire.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions none. Row states are meaningless with respect to the claim and are best treated as cannot_determine. Relation 'discusses' is a loose fit: the paper discusses monosemanticity generally but not this claim. 'cites_only' does not apply either, since neither original is cited. Some readers might take the remark against relying on top-activating examples as bearing on V6. It concerns SAE latents and POS labels, though, and the paper never tests whether an explanation predicts held-out firing, so it gets no verdict. Omitting the random-label control and dense baselines from rows is acceptable, since they bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit, neuron-pole explanations, or shares of poles assigned one, two, or unknown jobs.
Only LLaMA-3-8B and one SAE are analyzed; no cross-model or scale comparison.
No InceptionV1 examples, pose interpretation, or recursive-generalization analysis.
No comparison of architecture, regularization, or explanation tools, and no interpretable-neuron share estimates.
No attribution graphs or test of whether model neurons suffice as circuit units.
No natural-language explanations evaluated for their ability to predict neuron firing beyond the examples used to create them.
No automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

source_check.notes: All four rows and the statement check out. The data are SAE latents on LLaMA-3-8B layer 30 (GUM), not neurons, so no version applies. Table 8: 11 of 17 categories have recall >=0.95 (X 0.727 lowest); D ranges 0.093 (INTJ) to 0.350. Appendix A.1 repeats this at layers 2 and 15 (L* 530/501; D 0.15/0.32).

statements.correction: Compact feature set L* (union of minimal coverage sets) has 498 latents, 12% shared between 2+ POS. Held-out recall mostly >=0.95. Mean D 0.27 (sd 0.07) vs 0.06 chance. Controlled data: mean over templates P 0.192, R 0.937, F1 0.318.
statements.problem: Numbers match the text at layer 30: 498 latents in the union L*, 12% shared, held-out recall mostly >=0.95, mean D 0.27 vs 0.06 chance, controlled P 0.192 and R 0.937. The controlled values are means over 12 templates, which is fine for a summary.
